article.headline: A Free Cloth Simulation Tool That Blender Has Long Needed
article.lede: Daniel Bystedt, a senior concept artist at Goodbye Kansas Studios and one of Blender's most prominent advocates, has released Bystedt's Cloth Builder at no cost. The add-on wraps Blender's native cloth physics in a cleaner interface, bundles readymade garments and collision characters, and removes much of the manual plumbing that slows production pipelines.
article.body:
Blender ships with a capable cloth simulator, but setting it up for a real garment — pinning fabric to a shoulder, coaxing a cape to drape believably over a figure — involves assembling several systems by hand: the Cloth modifier, vertex groups to control stiffness, collision objects, weight painting. Bystedt's Cloth Builder automates that scaffolding. Artists choose a quality level, assign colliders, and run the simulation from a single panel rather than hunting across Blender's property tabs.

The add-on's pinning tools are a particular improvement. **Pinning** locks chosen vertices to a fixed point in space so they don't fall with gravity — the mechanism that holds a shirt collar or a cloak clasp in place. The native workflow requires manually managing vertex groups for this; Bystedt's tool lets artists click any vertex in the viewport and pin or unpin it interactively. The add-on also supports self-collision (preventing cloth from passing through itself) and pressure simulation for inflatable objects.

A practical time-saver is the *Shape Key* workflow. At any frame in a simulation, artists can save the cloth's deformed state as a Shape Key — a stored mesh pose — and use it as the starting shape for a new simulation. This lets a team iterate on mid-simulation poses without re-running the full sequence from the beginning.

The bundled asset library distinguishes the release from a bare-bones utility. Included are capes, trousers, and sweaters — pre-configured for simulation — alongside male and female armature characters built specifically as collision objects. A **Geometry Nodes** setup accompanies the clothing assets; it procedurally generates cloth thickness, splits garment pieces at their seams, and UV-unwraps them, tasks that would otherwise occupy a rigger for hours.

Bystedt has form for this kind of generosity. Bystedt's Blender Baker, his earlier public release, streamlined texture-map baking. Both tools arrive free on Gumroad, and both reflect a pattern in Blender's community: artists who built careers in expensive proprietary software, converted to Blender before its 2.80 overhaul, and now contribute tooling back. The add-on is available directly from the artist's Gumroad page.

concepts.definition: A physics component in Blender that simulates how a mesh behaves as fabric — responding to gravity, wind, and collisions with other objects. It is computationally expensive and requires careful parameter tuning to produce believable results.

In cloth simulation, a designated mesh that the cloth cannot pass through. A character's body is typically set as a collision object so garments drape over it rather than falling straight through the geometry.

A stored snapshot of a mesh's vertex positions in Blender. Artists blend between Shape Keys to animate deformations or, as in this add-on, use a mid-simulation pose as the starting point for a new physics run.

Blender's node-based procedural modelling system, introduced in version 2.92. It allows non-destructive, programmable manipulation of mesh data — thickness, seam splitting, UV layout — without manually editing the underlying geometry.

A named selection of vertices on a mesh, each assigned a weight between 0 and 1. Physics modifiers read these weights to vary properties like cloth stiffness or pinning strength across different parts of a garment.
